Lion (Doctrine)
LY-un
n.
Old English lēo, from Latin leo; Hebrew ’arī, k’phīr, lábī’ (several Hebrew words for lion, distinguished by age and characteristic); Greek leōn. The lion in Scripture is an extensive metaphor governing both Christ as the Lion of the tribe of Judah and Satan as the roaring lion seeking to devour.

📖 Biblical Definition

The lion in Scripture is one of the great paired-metaphors, governing both Christ and Satan in starkly opposite registers. Christ is the Lion of the tribe of Judah; Satan is the roaring lion seeking to devour. The OT lion-references are extensive and varied. Jacob’s prophetic blessing on Judah (Gen 49:9-10): Judah is a lion’s whelp: from the prey, my son, thou art gone up: he stooped down, he couched as a lion, and as an old lion; who shall rouse him up? The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come. The lion-imagery is here tied to the Messianic prophecy: from Judah’s tribe shall come the Lion who is the King. The Psalms use lion-imagery for both holy and unholy purposes: the LORD as the Lion of Zion (Hos 11:10; Amos 3:8); enemies as lions seeking to tear (Ps 7:2; 10:9; 17:12; 22:13, 21; 35:17; 57:4; 91:13). Daniel is delivered from the literal lions’ den (Dan 6); the Babylonian empire is figured as a lion in Dan 7:4. The New Testament fulfillment of the Lion-of-Judah prophecy is in Revelation 5:5: and one of the elders saith unto me, Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book, and to loose the seven seals thereof. The Lion of Judah is the One who has prevailed (the same Greek root as nikaō, to overcome)—Christ in His victorious power, opening the seals of God’s sealed book, executing the eschatological purposes of the Father. The striking feature of Rev 5 is the immediate identification of this Lion with the Lamb that was slain (v. 6): the One who is the Lion of Judah is also the Lamb in the midst of the throne. The two metaphors stand together—meek Lamb who was slain, mighty Lion who has prevailed—in the one Christ. The other great NT lion-reference is 1 Peter 5:8, applied not to Christ but to Satan: be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour. The devil’s lion-imagery is the perfect opposite of Christ’s: not the Lion of Judah whose victory is the salvation of His people, but the roaring lion of the adversary whose purpose is the devouring of the saints. The believer is therefore caught between two lions: the Lion of Judah who has prevailed for him, and the roaring lion who walks about seeking to devour him. The biblical pastoral application is direct: stand in the strength of the Lion of Judah; resist the roaring lion who, though terrible, has already been overcome by Christ’s prevailing.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines LION as a quadruped of the genus Felis, very strong, fierce, and rapacious; in scripture, the extensive paired metaphor of Christ as the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Rev 5:5) who has prevailed, and Satan as the roaring lion (1 Pet 5:8) who walks about seeking whom he may devour.

LION, n. — A quadruped of the genus Felis, very strong, fierce, and rapacious. In scripture, applied to Christ (the Lion of the tribe of Judah, Rev 5:5) and to the devil (the roaring lion, 1 Pet 5:8).

LIONESS, n. — The female of the lion kind.

📖 Key Scripture

Revelation 5:5 — "And one of the elders saith unto me, Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book, and to loose the seven seals thereof."

Genesis 49:9-10 — "Judah is a lion’s whelp: from the prey, my son, thou art gone up: he stooped down, he couched as a lion, and as an old lion; who shall rouse him up? The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come."

1 Peter 5:8 — "Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour."

Hosea 11:10 — "They shall walk after the LORD: he shall roar like a lion: when he shall roar, then the children shall tremble from the west."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The lion-doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by the loss of the Christ-as-Lion-of-Judah teaching in much contemporary preaching (which has often retained Christ-as-Lamb and lost Christ-as-Lion, producing an unbalanced Christology)—and on the other by the loss of the devil-as-roaring-lion-of-1-Peter-5 register that has muted the seriousness of the spiritual warfare every saint actually faces.

expand to see more

The loss of the Christ-as-Lion-of-Judah teaching has produced, in much contemporary preaching, an unbalanced Christology that retains Christ-as-Lamb and quietly drops Christ-as-Lion. The meek Lamb is preached; the mighty Lion is muted; the believer hears regularly of Christ’s sacrificial love and rarely of His conquering kingship. Revelation 5 refuses the imbalance. The Lion of the tribe of Judah and the Lamb that was slain are the same Christ; the Lion has prevailed precisely as the Lamb who was slain; the Lamb is also the Lion who opens the seals and executes the Father’s eschatological purposes. The recovery is the recovery of the full Christological substance: the meek Lamb is also the mighty Lion; the One who was slain for our sins is the same One who has prevailed and reigns as Lord of lords and King of kings. The unbalanced Lamb-only Christology produces a sentimentalized Christ; the balanced Lion-and-Lamb Christology produces the substantive Christ the apostles and the church across the ages have worshipped.

The opposite corruption is the loss of the devil-as-roaring-lion register. Peter’s sober warning—be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour—is taken with insufficient seriousness in much contemporary preaching that has either disbelieved in a personal devil altogether (the liberal-theological loss) or treated him as a figure of folklore from which contemporary Christians can be largely exempt (the comfort-culture loss). Peter’s instruction is to be sober and vigilant precisely because the adversary is real, walks about, and seeks to devour. The recovery is the recovery of biblical realism about the spiritual warfare every saint actually faces. The believer is caught between two lions: the Lion of Judah who has prevailed for him, and the roaring lion of the adversary who seeks to devour him. To know both is to live in the substantive register the apostles assumed: stand in the strength of the prevailing Lion; resist the roaring lion in the faith that knows he has been overcome by Christ; sober and vigilant, in the warfare that is real, on the side of the Lion who has already won.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew lion-terms (’arī, k’phīr, lábī’, etc.); Greek leōn; the great paired metaphor of Christ as the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Rev 5:5; Gen 49:9-10) who has prevailed for His people, and Satan as the roaring lion (1 Pet 5:8) who walks about seeking to devour them.

expand to see more

Hebrew ’arī (H738) — lion (general term; over 70 OT uses).

Hebrew k’phīr (H3715) — young lion (vigorous, in its strength).

Greek leōn (G3023) — lion (9 NT uses; Heb 11:33, 2 Tim 4:17, Rev 4:7; 5:5; 9:8, 17; 10:3; 13:2; 1 Pet 5:8).

Hebrew Shīlōh (H7886) — Shiloh (the messianic title of Gen 49:10, behind whose coming the lion-of-Judah prophecy stands).

Usage

"Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed—Rev 5:5’s fulfillment of Gen 49:9-10’s lion-of-Judah Messianic prophecy."

"Your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour—1 Pet 5:8’s sober warning about the spiritual warfare every saint faces."

"Loss of Christ-as-Lion produces unbalanced Lamb-only Christology; loss of devil-as-roaring-lion produces unrealistic comfort-culture spirituality; biblical lion-doctrine holds both lions in their proper places."
